summary: Defines procedures and protocol mechanisms to measure packet loss, one-way and two-way delay, and related metrics in MPLS networks. Providers need these measurements to monitor service level agreements and for planning and troubleshooting.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6374 defines messages that measure packet loss and delay across MPLS paths. The two ends exchange counters or timestamps so an operator can estimate how the path performs.

questions: what is mpls loss and delay measurement
how is packet loss measured in mpls
what is the difference between direct and inferred loss measurement
subtitle: Defines MPLS messages for measuring packet loss, delay, and related performance metrics.

tldr.problem: Network operators need agreed ways to measure packet loss and delay across MPLS paths. The results support service monitoring, planning, and troubleshooting.
tldr.mechanism: A querier sends loss-measurement or delay-measurement messages over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel. A responder adds counters or timestamps and returns the message when a response is requested.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines direct and inferred loss measurement, delay measurement, and related procedures. It is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7214.

today: RFC 6374 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2011. It has been updated by RFC 7214.

sections.title: What the Measurements Are For
sections.content:
RFC 6374 defines two related protocols for MPLS networks: Loss Measurement (LM) and Delay Measurement (DM). They are designed to support hardware processing and can be used on Label Switched Paths, pseudowires, and MPLS sections.

Operators can use the protocols continuously or on demand. The RFC also describes measurements related to throughput and delay variation, plus unidirectional and loopback cases.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives network operators a way to measure loss and delay on MPLS paths. The same message formats also support related measurements, such as throughput.

sections.title: How Queries Measure Loss and Delay
sections.content:
In the basic bidirectional procedure, a querier sends a query to a responder and receives a response. For loss measurement, the two ends add their transmit and receive packet counts. The querier compares changes between successive messages because the counters at the two ends may not start at the same value.

For delay measurement, the query and response carry four timestamps: when the query leaves and arrives, and when the response leaves and arrives. One-way delay requires synchronized clocks at the two ends. The RFC's two-way channel delay calculation does not require synchronized clocks.
sections.plainLanguage: The ends compare packet counts to estimate loss and record send and receive times to measure delay. One-way delay needs synchronized clocks; two-way delay does not.

sections.title: Direct and Inferred Loss Measurement
sections.content:
In direct mode, the counters track data-plane packets on the measured channel. This can provide perfect loss accounting, but accurate operation may require special hardware and it applies only to some LSP types.

In inferred mode, the counters track generated test messages or other packets used as a proxy for data traffic. This gives approximate loss accounting but is generally applicable. The RFC leaves the definition of test protocols and proxy packets outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Direct measurement counts the actual traffic but may need specialized hardware. Inferred measurement counts test or proxy packets and gives an approximate result.

sections.title: Message Formats and Timestamps
sections.content:
LM and DM messages travel over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel. The MPLS label stack ends with the Generic Associated Channel Label, followed by an Associated Channel Header that identifies the message type.

Messages contain a common set of fields for version, flags, control code, and length, followed by counters or timestamps and an optional block of Type-Length-Value objects. The RFC defines timestamp formats for a null value, a sequence number, NTP version 4, and the low-order 64 bits of the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol format. The IEEE 1588 format is the required default.
sections.plainLanguage: The message header identifies what measurement is being made. The message then carries counters or timestamps, with optional extra fields.

sections.title: Running a Measurement Session
sections.content:
A session is a sequence of queries for one channel, controlled by the querier and identified by a shared session identifier. The querier can request a response over the measured channel, over an out-of-band channel, or no response.

The Session Query Interval TLV lets the querier learn the responder's minimum supported query interval. The querier then selects an interval no shorter than that value. Responders should limit query rates, and the querier should suspend a sustained measurement if too many responses are lost.

LM depends on state from successive messages, so lost or misordered messages can make an interval unmeasurable. DM does not use this counter-delta state.
sections.plainLanguage: The querier sets the session and how often it sends queries. If replies are lost or arrive out of order, some loss intervals cannot be measured reliably.

sections.title: Load, Disclosure, and Security
sections.content:
Frequent measurement adds traffic and work for both network devices and endpoints. Operators should choose rates that do not unduly stress resources, and responders should rate-limit incoming queries. Implementations are required to disclose their supported metrics, channel types, query intervals, counter sizes, timestamp formats, and other measurement characteristics.

The RFC assumes the MPLS path and far-end identity have already been checked by existing mechanisms. Where that is not available, implementations should be able to disable these channel types. The messages remain vulnerable to injection and man-in-the-middle attacks; basic checks can detect implausible response values. IPsec is recommended for out-of-band responses over IP.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurement traffic must not create excessive load. Operators should also verify the path and peer before trusting the results.
